In the case of grocery supplies in Quebec I think only two Conservatives were asked to tender for the annual supplies. That was the system of tender which was adopted not only in this department but, I am satisfied, in every other department of the Conservative administration which was a purchaser of goods in any quantity or to any extent. Was my hon. friend a party to it? Did he know about it? Did he administer that pernicious system? I have some public records which I shall lay before the House, in that respect, not all the records I would like to lay before the House, because, as I intimated, the great fire in the western block wiped the slate clear prior to 1887. The first document I submit in order to show the connection of my hon. friend with this iniquitous, this atrocious patronage system which the Conservatives operated in this country for eighteen years, is an extract from the evidence of Mr. Gregory, to be found in volume 8, page 3275, of the evidence taken by Mr. Justice Cassels when conducting his commission of inquiry. It is there stated:
I will produce you letters from tlie different ministers thanking me for the aid I gave them in carrying on the business, from the very first minister of the Marine and Fisheries Department, a Conservative: from the next minister, a Liberal; Mr. Albert Smith, Mr. McClennan, Mr. Pope, and even one from Foster-to the best of my knowledge, the celebrated Foster.
That is the evidence of Mr. Gregory taken from the official report. I have stated and I desire to state it again that my hon. friend while he did preside over the Department of Marine and Fisheries, was warned by the Auditor General that the system of purchasing supplies in that department was not a proper one. He .was warned by his deputy minister that it was an improper system, and by Mr. Gregory, his purchasing agent. I refer to the report of the Auditor General for 1886, and to a communication dated August 31, of that year, as follows:
Sir,-I was recently at Quebec and visited the office of your agent there. I find that the supplies purchased by Mr. Gregory are not obtained under contract, and the prices paid are apparently higher than those which are paid for the same kind of goods purchased for the marine hospital under contract. The difference probably arises from tenders be-

ing called for in the latter case and not in the former.
I beg to request that Mr. Gregory be instructed to call for tenders for all the principal supplies required by him.
That letter must have come in some way or other to the attention of my hon. friend while he was minister in control of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. Did he regard it? Did he carry out the suggestion? I may say not, as later documents will show.
I shall refer again to the report of the Cassels' Commission at volume 5, page 1394: This language, which I now quote, is the language of Mr. Watson, who was the counsel before the commission, and I do not submit it as evidence, but the documents to which he alludes I do submit. Mr. Watson says:
And the correspondence prior to that in the department, your lordship will recollect as a matter of history, was all destroyed in the lire that took place, so that there is really nothing beyond 1887 that is of record. I find they are all of this nature, and just as an illustration I run over a few of these to show your lordship the character of it.
On May 13, 1887, a letter was directed to the Hon. G. E. Foster, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries Department, saying:
My Dear Mr. Foster,-I beg to recommend that the firm of Powers & Co., machinists, Halifax, should be put on the list.
It did not say what list, just should be put on the list.

and receive a share of the work to be
done on all kinds of sheet metal work for steamships, lighthouses, etc.
Yours faithfully
(Signed) T. E. KENNY.
I believe at that time he was the sitting member for Halifax. The note on the foot says:
'Put this on the list.'
(Signed) G. E. FOSTER.
Another note-
Done, and letter written to Mr. Kenny.
That letter was written in 1887, a long time ago, my hon. friends may say, but I am only citing it to show that the system was a complete one, a hard and fast system. Conservatives only could supply goods, but in the first place they must be put on a preferred list at the recommendation of a leading Conservative. When they were placed on that list they were entitled to receive tender papers, to go through the form at least of tendering, and in the end to secure, no doubt, a large share of government money.
There is another letter from Charlottetown, P.E.I., on January 6, 1887, directed Mr. GUTHRIE.
again to my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster). This letter says:
I have to acknowledge your kind note of the 15th ult., and beg to say Mr. Lord has not carried out your instuctions. nor for some reason best known to himself will he do so without a peremptory order. As you will see by reference to the December invoices for supplies to the department here which, T have reason to believe, are very large. I regret to take up one moment of your valuable time, knowing it is occupied with much more momentous matters looking towards Washington, but to the party interests here it is of some little importance.
I am, sir,
Yours respectfully,

The note on that letter addressed to my hon. friend is:
Ask Mr. Lord if he has followed out the minister's instructions as to patronage, and why Mr. Dawson has not yet received any order.
This shows that according to the minister's view of the system which then existed, the order should go to Mr. Lord, although the amount spoken of was a large amount, or the order to be given was a large order.
I turn now to a letter written by Mr. Gregory in 1887. I am not very positive at what time my hon. friend was transferred from the Department of Marine and Fisheries to some other department, but I think he was there when this letter was written. It is a letter from Mr. Gregory to the deputy minister, as follows:
October 13, 1887.
Sir,-Referring to your letter of the 11th inst., calling my attention and asking explanation about prices of hay, etc., I have to call your attention to my letter of the 15th Februarv, 1887, and several others on the same subject, supplies. It has long been my humble opinion, and I have no reason yet to change it, that all supplies, of whatsoever nature or kind, should be thrown freely open to public competition and given to the party whose tender would prove most advantageous at fixed prices for one or more years. As the matter has heretofore stood I am ordered to purchase from certain parties who owe this fact entirely to powerful influence: prices, it is true, are fixed for most articles, but it has become the opinion of traders that none but certain friends can get the patronage, whatever political party is in power, Liberal or Conservative. The result is very little competition.
This letter was signed by Mr. Gregory and was evidently laid before the deputy minister. The deputy minister also made a similar recommendation to the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), who was in charge of that department at that date and who disregarded that, as he had disregarded the intimation from the Auditor General.

On January 31, 1887, a telegram was sent addressed to Wm. Smith, Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
I wish that as usual, paint, powder, oils, drugs, common stationery for lighthouses, groceries, hardware aDd dry goods be purchased in Quebec, also provisions at once.
(Sgd.) HECTOR L. LANGEVIN.
On the 5th of February, 1887, a somewhat guarded letter was written by Mr. Foster, to the deputy minister at St. John. He says:
In the matter of Sir Hector's telegram, saying to continue purchase of material for lighthouses as usual in Quebec, keeping the amount purchased small. It is not necessary now to lay in a heavy stock. Stationery must be got at the stationery office. Not necessary to buy paints and oils for lighthouses at present.

Continue usual patronage, Baudet and Chinic, Quebec, with conditions as per letter sent concerning Sir Hector's request. Inform Caron.
(Sgd.) G. E. FOSTER.
These letters show that the whole system was one recognized by every branch of the government. We have here recommendations by the then Minister of Public Works, Sir Hector Langevin. We have also a former minister, Sir Adolphe Caron, associated with the system. I think, therefore, I may fairly say that the system, in all its heinousness and iniquity, was recognized as the basic principle for the transaction of general business by the Conservative administration of those days. Might I put a question on behalf of the new _members of this House? Are we to take it for granted that the reading of these letters, written by men who are dead and gone years ago, justifies the deplorable patronage system of the present day?

I trust my hon. friend from Lanark (Mr. Thoburn) will remain and listen to the balance of my remarks because I think he will very fairly get from them justification for any system which exists to-day.

1 do not know that I can find any cases precisely similar to the ones mentioned by my hon. friend, but I have some that come so near them that I think he will admit the principle is the same. I find a striking instance of the employment of the middle-man and a man who, I think, was not in the trade. I refer to this because of the question asked me by my hon. friend from York, New Brunswick,

I wish to say that I have been engaged in the fresh meat and grocery business for over twenty years, I have had the honour of meeting you on two occasions, though perhaps you cannot recall me now. I have supported the Liberal-Conservative party since 1878, from conviction. Dean & O'Neal, two very selfish gentlemen, cut the price down, so that there is nothing in it, and there they have recourse to furnishing an inferior article. I was side-tracked last year on one-half cent per pound, and I have put in a tender this year for 8 cents for beef, which is a very moderate price. I have not heard whether my tender was lowest or not. My main object in troubling you with this communication is to inform you how the matter of supply is regarded by those who tender, including myself, that is that the meat supply should be equally divided amongst us, by the department here. And so the letters go, fifty or a hundred more, which I do not need to read to the House. My only object is to show to what extent the evil of patronage had permeated the whole business system of the late Conservative administration, and how that evil patronage system existed under the very eye, - and management, and control of my hon. friend from North Toronto, and he never raised his voice in protest. Now, Sir, it is well known that when the change of government took place in 1896, there were conditions existing in Canada which called for treatment at the hands of the in-coming administration. I do not say that the government may not be open to some criticism for having neglected, during a number of years, the question of patronage, and the mode in which goods were supplied to the government. They carried out the old Conservative system far too long, in my estimation. But this may be offered, I take it, by way of excuse, by way of palliation, that the system was inherited by
them, they did not make it, they did not inaugurate it, it was there, operated by the Conservatives. They had before them the report of the Civil Service Commission of 1892 saying that, so far as the commissioners were able to find, the business was being fairly well conducted, the officials were performing their duties; and two departments in particular, the Marine and Fisheries Department and the Militia Department. which subsequently came in for some vigorous treatment, were specially mentioned by the commissioners in 1892 as being well conducted. The government, having a great many very important measures to deal with, might well overlook the question of patronage, for a few years, at all events. The government had, in the first place, to look after the condition of the country-trade stagnant and declining, markets cut off and new markets to'be sought, tariffs to be revised, the gold excitement in the west to be provided for, the South African war, the construction of the Transcontinental railway, the establishment of the two new provinces-these were works of great magnitude which the government had to undertake, and for some years no doubt the government did allow the old Conservative system to remain in the various departments in connection with the transaction of public business. There is this also to be said, that the government, by its own motion, unasked by any one, undertook to remedy the defect, and after having found a remedy, has been the first government, so far as I have been able to find, in Canada that ever applied a remedy with any idea of effecting a cure.
In the spring of 1907 the government certainly became aware there were irregularities, that there was wrong-doing in connection with some of the departments. Whether that knowledge was gained by the government on account of disclosures in the Public Accounts Committee or not I cannot say, but certainly it is that in the month of May, 1907, the government, of its own motion, appointed a commission of investigation, not only into the circumstances of the Civil Service, but also to look into the methods adopted by the various departments. The powers given to the commissioners were of the widest, just as full and wide as were the powers given to the commission of 1892, but there is this difference between the two commissions. The commission of 1892 deliberately refused to examine into the business transactions of the various departments, stating in the first page of their report that they refused to do so, while the commission of 1907 deliberately set about such an examination, and I think it is wrell that they did set about it. During the following year the commission reported that certain abuses existed. I need not go over them; they

are all familiar to the hon. members of this House. That commission made certain specific recommendations, many of which recommendations have since been carried into effect. Some of the recommendations it made I may refer.to briefly. In the first place, it made suggestions as to the mode of dealing with estimates by committees of the House of Commons, proposing that the English system be adopted. I believe that that question is one which in all probability will come up at a very early date. It is a question which should come up because I am satisfied that a better system could be adopted with regard to estimates and the expenditure of money, not in the departments, but in this House and in the committees of this House. A second recommendation was that stringent measures should be taken to suppress those abuses which they found existed in one or two of the departments and to punish the offenders. The government has taken action in that regard. It introduced an amendment to the Criminal Code to meet the views of the commissioners, amendments similar to those to be found in the English Act called ' An Act for the prevention of corruption ' passed in 1906 by the imperial House. The next recommendation of the commissioners was for the removal of the Civil Service from political influences. The first step ever taken in this country in this regard was taken by this government within the last year or eighteen months. The commission recommended the appointment of a Civil Service Board. That has been established, the inside service has been placed under that board and I for one look forward to the day, and at no distant time, when, I believe, that Act will be made applicable to the major portion of the outside service. That commission further recommended the abolition of the patronage lists in the various departments.
Has that been carried out?	' !

Yes. I am going to say that in so far as it is possible to carry out the recommendation in that respect It has been carried out and there i3 no patronage list, either under the name of a patronage list or under any other name, existing today 'in any department of the present government.
I would like to hear a minister say that.

Perhaps you will hear that too. All the recommendations of a practical kind that could be carried out have been carried out by the government. We have now just such a service, just such a business administration as this commission suggested. But, further than that, we had the report of Mr. Justice Cassels. His recommenda-Mr. GUTHRIE.
tions were largely a reiteration of the suggestions of the previous commission with one addition. Mr. Justice Cassels suggested that in addition to the other recommendations the government should establish a purchasing board which should purchase all the supplies of the different departments of the government. That board has not been constituted. That recommendation has not been carried out. It may be in the future, but another system has been instituted, and one which I think is giving entire satisfaction, or has, at all events, given entire satisfaction up to the present time. That is the appointment of responsible persons to act as purchasing agents in each of the great purchasing or spending, departments. Whether a board of three, or four, or five individuals with authority to make all the purchases would be better than one, two or three individual purchasing agents for the various departments is a matter upon which there may be two opinions. Personally I prefer the form adopted by the government and to-day in the Department of Railways and Canals you will find that every five cents worth of goods purchased in that department, the largest spending department in the administration, is purchased through a single man, Mr. Lavoie, the purchasing agent. What is the principle adopted? Let me say, in the first place, that about a year ago positive instructions were given for the abolition of the patronage list. I can only take the word of Mr. Lavoie, who appears to be a most upright and intelligent man and he assures me, and other officials assure me on their honour, that no such thing exists in that department to-day, and that no favour is shown to Liberal or Conservative with respect to any purchase that may be made. That is the principle upon which purchases are made and the only purchases which are not made in that way in the great department of Railways and Canals are what might be termed emergency purchases, because you cannot devise a system which can provide, in the case of a broken lock or a broken pane of glass, that you shall go out and get competitive prices.

Tenders for bar iron and steel are treated a little differently again, the specification being made out according to requisition received in Moncton and the leading firms in the production of bar iron all being asked to tender. There are nine on the list, I do not know their political leanings. These nine firms were all asked for prices on bar iron and the lowest tender was accepted. So with the tenders for paints and colours, brushes and brooms and rubber goods, all of which I shall lay on the table.
My hon. friend from New Brunswick asked whether some professional man in Moncton was supplying hardware to the government. I think he has reference to supplies of the Canadian Gutta Percha Company.
I refer to Dr. Murray.

Supplied by Dr. Murray. Last year the purchases ran something like $12,000. If the hon. member will turn up the Auditor General's Report, he will find in the items included in the list of purchases that the purchases from Dr. Murray consisted of the manufacture of rubber and gutta nercha and the largest amount of them were hose. It happens that Dr. Murray is the agent for the Canadian Gutta Percha Company for the province of New Brunswick. The tender was received direct from Dr. Murray. His was the lowest tender received and he obtained the order. He advertises himself and states he is the agent oi the Canadian Gutta-Percha Company for New Brunswick, and I believe that in all its parts that is a thoroughly Conservative company. That is the explanation I have received in regard to these purchases, and I may tell my hon. friend, although he is a member of the legal profession, that if he wishes to tender for hardware or oil and is the lowest tenderer he will undoubtedly receive the order, just as Mr. Murray did.
You can count me out.

I submit also the list of those who were asked to tender for cement, including, I think, all the cement firms in Canada. So for fencing, including, I fancy, all the manufacturers in Canada, so for tinware, so for passenger coach wheels, so for axles, fire brick, oak lumber, hard pine lumber and electric wiring. The supply of coal, I think, is about the onlv other large order for goods which the Department of Railways and Canals give. That supply is dealt with on a different principle. I do not know that it is altogether a correct one but it is a fair one. Coal mining is one of the native Mr. GUTHRIE.
industries of the maritime provinces, and it is the desire of the government to give all a fair share of the patronage. Instead of calling for tenders the government arbitrarily fixes the price of coal at so much per ton and divides its orders among the different companies, and those companies which will not contract at that fixed price do not receive the order. As a rule, however, the orders are distributed among all the collieries in the maritime provinces. But leaving out coal and taking all the other large purchases of that department, they are all controlled by a single man. If there be any wrong-doing or abuse or irregularity, you can put your finger on the responsible party, Mr. Lavoie, the purchasing agent.
I thought the hon. gentleman said the government fixed the price. Does he mean the government or the Intercolonial Railway Commission?
I fancy the department fixes it.
What is the price?

I do not know the prices down there, but writh the exception of coal everything is bought on a system of fair and open competiton. There is no patronage list, no spoils system. The virus condemned by my hon. friend from North Toronto has not entered into that department at all events. I would ask hon. gentlemen opposite if they can suggest any improved system. Any improvement which they can offer will be warmly welcomed, I am sure, by the government, and my hon. friend who presides over the Department of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham).
Does that system apply to any other department?

Yes. It is argued that a purchasing board can do better than a purchasing agent. In England they have a purchasing board. The system is a good one, but it is the most expensive in any part of the world. It may be fairly argued that an individual, trained in a department, knowing its requirements, year by year becoming more familiar with the amounts required and the prices-it may be fairly argued that such an individual can do better in the interests of the department, can judge better what is required, and what prices should be paid, than any three or four gentlemen constituting a board. I think that is the view the government takes because the various departments are having each its own purchasing agent. Under the British system there is tremendous waste. There is an annual sale of the government surplus goods-goods purchased far in excess of the requirements. And I am not now talking of war or naval supplies,

which are always purchased in excess of requirements, but of general supplies. The British government has each year a large supply of excess stores which will not keep and has to auction these off, and goods which cost $2 or $3 a pound have been actually sold at three pence a pound. That is a statement which has been made to me by an English official. It may be that a better system can be devised than the one we are following. If so let us have it. Let me turn to the Marine and Fisheries Department, which came so much under fire. In that department there is no patronage list whatever. That list was abolished, as Mr. Justice Cassels mentions in his report, about October, 1908. Furthermore, the instructions of the minister are that no patronage list shall be permitted to exist; that all goods shall be bought in the open market. The department advertises in the newspapers, except in the case of small supplies which cannot be bought by tender. These small supplies, which are called emergency supplies, are purchased by the agent in the open market, at what he considers a fair price; and if he be an honest man, he will get the lowest price. You have to trust some one. All the lighthouse supplies, fog signal service and ship supplies are now purchased after advertising for tenders in the newspapers, and the contracts given to the lowest tenderers.
Is that advertising done in the same way?

I intend touching upon that if I can get time. If anything goes wrong in the present system, who is responsible? Mr. Doutre, the purchasing agent, says that he is, and I certainly think he would be. A more intelligent, capable officer it would be hard to find. He has been a long time in the department, he knows offhand the market prices of the goods he has to deal with and he cannot be fooled, though of course he might be particeps criminis, but nothing short of actual dishonesty can cause loss to the department as at present managed.
The Department of Justice controls all the supplies for the various penitentiaries of Canada. The patronage list in that department, if it ever existed, has been abolished, and it has its purchasing agent. This is the first year that system has been put in force, and we do not know what the result will be, but the department has done away with the political pull and is making its purchases in the open market. The same can be said of the Department of the Interior. That is not a large purchasing department, but the Indian branch of it does make considerable purchases. Every dollar's worth purchased by that branch, except in the case of the very distant reserves, is purchased after advertising in the newspaper for tenders. The goods purchased are principally agricultural implements, provisions, clothing and cattle. In the case of some of the reserves, which are very distant there are but two companies which can tender-Revillon Bros., and the Hudson Bay Company, and one or the other gets the contract. But in the case of the nearer reserves there are publie advertisements and there is no patronage list, and the lowest tenderer gets the order. If hon. members opposite can suggest a better system, let them do so. I was greatly-disappointed when I found that the hon, member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) after condemning the system as vigorously as he did, after showing what evil results might follow, suggested no improvement, no way out of the difficulty. The right hon. the Prime Minister asked him what he would do but he made no suggestion. I think that the government may well be congratulated on the advance they have made in the past two or three years and the alacrity and courage they have shown in acting on the recommendations of the two commissions. Other commissions were issued from time \o time-one in 1880, one, a commission of ministers of the Crown, in 1889 or 1890, and another in 1892. All these commissions made their recommendations and suggestions; and, no doubt, had these been carried out at the time it would have done immeasurable good. But every one of them was neglected, the abuses were allowed to continue until they culminated in the revelations in the Public Accounts Committee of this House in 1891. This government has been, at all events courageous it may be at the price of political support and in the face of political friends. It has adopted a new system, as I have shown; and the patronage system as it existed until two years ago exist no longer in the various departments of this government. We all know that difficulties exist-and how to remedy them I do not know-in the outside service in regard to political appointments. How can these be remedied? I trust that the Civil Service Act will be extended in the near future to the outside service. But even then, as the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) has pointed out, there will still be some 15,000 to 20,000 people to whom it will not apply- the dav labourer, the casual employee, and all these men may well be classed as belonging to a patronage system. But how are you going to overcome that? I do not know the remedy, and the hon. member for North Toronto has not suggested it. But what the House should do under present circumstances is not to condemn the course adopted by the government as this motion proposes; not to sav that the present system 'constitutes a menace to honest

and efficient government', as the resolution says; not to say that the present system 'incites too great waste of the resources and extravagance of expenditures', as the resolution says; or that it 'tends inevitably to corrupt and lower the tone of public morals', as the resolution says. Every step the government has taken has been taken in the direction of improving the service, of stopping the waste where there was waste, and of raising, not lowering, public morals. And I trust that in their future efforts-and their efforts will continue no doubt-they will have the support from my hon. friend from North Toronto and other hon. members on that side of the House which they are entitled to expect. We have not a perfect system-no one says we have. There are a great many points yet to be covered. There is, for instance, the question of newspaper advertising. And let me tell you that it is not correct to say that the advertisements of this government appear only in the Liberal press. For instance, take the advertisements for contracts on the Intercolonial. How does the government proceed? At Moncton, there was a twelve-engine house to be built. Advertisements were posted, at every station, of course, but advertisements also were put in nine or ten newspapers, and at the very top of the list, and receiving the highest price is the Halifax 'Herald'. That cannot be classed as a government supporter. I have seen government advertisements again and again in other Conservative newspapers. At the same time I admit that the rule is very largely to give the printing patronage to the newspapers supporting the government. I do not know how long that will continue, but there is more justification for this than for buying goods at fictitious prices or under fictitious tenders from) vour friends, which was the system up to 1896. It is but natural to dislike giving favours to * press that, day after day, misrepresents your public accounts and makes charges against your government, many of them unfounded. It is human nature-you do not like to pamper such a press. There may be some sort of justification for having a patronage list so far as this matter is concerned. So long as publicity can be sufficiently obtained through the Liberal newspapers, I would say let the advertising be given to the Liberal newspapers. But when publicity cannot be gained in this way, then resort to the Conservative newspapers or to the ' Canada Gazette ' which ever you like. But the resolution sufcT-mitted by the hon. member for North Toronto condemns the present government and the prevailing system, and I submit this should not be done. Instead of con-Mr. GUTHRIE.
demning we should commend the government for what they have been able to do; instead of denouncing the system we should congratulate the government for having made advance, distinct and I trust permanent advance, in improving the whole business administration of the various departments. And, with that view, I conclude my remarks by apologizing for the great length of time I have occupied, and by moving, seconded by Mr. Tolmie:
That all the words after the word ' that ' in the said resolution be struck out, and the following substituted in place thereof:- This House approves the rapid advance made by the government toward the elimination of the system of party patronage which has been in operation under every administration since confederation, and views with satisfaction the policy now in force of making all important purchases by public competition and tender.

Mr. Speaker, this being Wednesday, a day on which, under the rules, the House adjourns at six o'clock, we have only about five minutes to consider this question further. I am not aware whether the object of the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) in the course of his interminable remarks on the history of the government purchases prior to 1896 and going back to 1878, was to kill time or to kill the discussion. But it is clearly impossible to discuss the matter now, and I suppose that, following the usual order, this will go to the bottom of the paper and so we shall not hear of it again this session. This makes it impossible for a member on this side to reply. It is so obvious that the party patronage system has permeated the body politic that any man has only to look about him to be aware of that fact. Yet, directly we approach the question from this side of the House and try to put it in such a way that men of all parties can deal with it, there is a hyper-sensitiveness at once shown that a personal attack is made on hon. gentlemen opposite, and they immediately shield themselves behind the walls of party. I conceive that it is our business to help a discussion of this kind if we can by lifting the whole discussion to a higher level than before. It is a most singular thing for the hon. member for South Wellington to quote documents-interminable documents-to the effect that the spoils system existed prior to 1896, but that it was abolished by the present government when it came into power in that year. The hon. gentleman states that in 1892 the Royal Commission on the Civil Service recommended certain things which the Conservative party deliberately refused to adopt. This is a strange argument in view of the fact that the trend of our criticism is directed to this government in connec-

lion with this very matter of the Civil Service when party patronage had eaten the heart out of the departments for thirteen or fourteen years. I have only to refer to the report of the commission for 1908 and to quote two short statements from that report to reply to what the hon. member (Mr. Guthrie) has stated. These commissioners, appointed by the present government said:
The public service, the commissioners believe, not only at Ottawa, but elsewhere throughout the dominion has fallen back during the last fifteen years.
And then, at page 26, there is the following:
It has been pointed out in the most simple way that this practice had been followed^ by everybody and it could not be altered. I our commissioners, however, consider that, while the practice was alwavs bad, yet through the great development of the country the extent was not so great as to become serious until of recent years.
The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat said that the whole thing was' a farce. Well, if it was a farce when it went on from 1878 to 1896, how much greater has the farce been even according to the words of their own commissioners, from 1896 down to the present time. If the Conservatives chastised the people with whips, the hon. gentlemen opposite since they have been in authority, have chastised the people with scorpions. I would recommend to the right hon. gentleman who sometimes leads this party the words of a friend of his in the old country, and I think they may very well be applied to his career since 1896. John Morley said, ' He who begins life by stifling convictions is in a fair way for ending it without any convictions to stifle.5 It being now six o'clock, I beg to move the adjournment of the debate.

Motion agreed to.
